newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FOCUS-NAB MARGINS STEADY, BUT COSTS STICKY.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-NAB MARGINS STEADY, BUT COSTS STICKY.

text.p: Australia's largest bank signalled on Monday that a two-year slide in interest margins had ended, but warned of an announcement within a month of big technology costs to eradicate the Year 2000 Millennium Bug.
A buoyant National Australia Bank (NAB) managing director Don Argus also said NAB remained very acquisitive and observers should not be surprised if the bank announced new alliances.
Argus told a Securities Institute briefing that annual results from the group's Australian operations would not disappoint because margins had stabilised in the fourth quarter.

"Our Australian financial services group is really through the peak of the lower margins and you can see it in the third quarter results, and I don't think you'll be disappointed when you see the full year's results," he said.

A price war in the home mortgage market, triggered by non-bank competitors funded by securitisation, has been the major profit worry for Australia's four major banks in the 18 months. NAB is the largest bank in terms of assets and profits.
The major banks have sliced about 120 basis points from their home lending margins, forcing banks to warn of flat profits and restraining analysts' growth forecasts.
Many analysts had forecast this year's mortgage margin cuts would begin to eat away at earnings in earnest later in 1997.
Argus said as recently as last month, as he released flat third quarter profit results, that there was continued pressure on margins.
But he told reporters after the Securities Institute briefing that he did not expect further margin reduction at NAB in the current final quarter of the year to September 30.
"At this stage, the margin erosion is stabilised," he said.

However, Argus warned that NAB's cost-cutting programme was not biting as fast or as hard as he wanted it to and that the market would have to expect lower returns on equity in the longer term because of ingrained low inflation.
"Our costs aren't coming down as quickly as I want them to," he told the audience of bankers, brokers and analysts.
He warned that costs to deal with the Year 2000 Millennium Bug had slowed NAB's push to cut its cost-to-income ratio to 40 percent from its current 54.8 percent.
"I wanted it by the year 2000, but you've got to deal with the Year 2000 technology issues around the globe so it will be a little longer, but not too much longer," he said.

Argus said he would advise the market in three to four weeks time on the cost to the bank of dealing with the Millennium Bug. Argus was adamant however that his oft-repeated 40 percent target remained. "The 40 percent stake in the ground is still real -- it's still there," he said, responding to some analysts' scepticism that the target was too ambitious.
Meanwhile, NAB would continue to look to grow by acquisition and through alliances like those it has with Mondex and HIH Winterthur.
"We're still an acquisitive bank, very much so," Argus said.
"Don't be surprised if we make announcements on other alliances on how we can push through product in other distribution channels."
He said trying to expand in the funds management business in particular through organic growth was too slow.

NAB's preferred target markets for acquisitions were Australia, the United States, Britain and Ireland. The Asian region was also a target market, he said. Argus denied that the prices for United States finance houses had risen too high.
Argus added that low inflation meant credit growth would remain slow and the market should adjust to lower return on equity rates than the recently achieved figure of 17 percent.
"We see a long-term sustainable figure of around the 15 percent mark," Argus said.
NAB's shares closed down 34 cents at A$19.29.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373 1800
